{{Short description|Mathematical sequence satisfying a specific pattern}}
{{distinguish|Arithmetic–geometric mean}}
{{Calculus |Series}}

In [[mathematics]], an '''arithmetico-geometric sequence''' is the result of element-by-element multiplication of the elements of a [[geometric progression]] with the corresponding elements of an [[arithmetic progression]]. The ''n''th element of an arithmetico-geometric sequence is the product of the ''n''th element of an arithmetic sequence and the ''n''th element of a geometric sequence.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Arithmetic-Geometric Progression {{!}} Brilliant Math & Science Wiki|url=https://brilliant.org/wiki/arithmetic-geometric-progression/|access-date=2021-04-21|website=brilliant.org|language=en-us}}</ref> An '''arithmetico-geometric series''' is a sum of terms that are the elements of an arithmetico-geometric sequence. Arithmetico-geometric sequences and series arise in various applications, such as the computation of [[expected values]] in [[probability theory]], especially in [[Bernoulli process|Bernoulli processes]].

For instance, the sequence

:<math>\frac{\color{blue}{0}}{\color{green}{1}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{1}}{\color{green}{2}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{2}}{\color{green}{4}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{green}{8}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{4}}{\color{green}{16}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{5}}{\color{green}{32}}, \cdots </math>

is an arithmetico-geometric sequence. The arithmetic component appears in the numerator (in {{color|blue|blue}}), and the geometric one in the denominator (in {{color|green|green}}). The [[Series (mathematics)|series]] summation of the infinite elements of this sequence has been called '''Gabriel's staircase''' and it has a value of 2.<ref name="Swain2018">{{cite journal|last1=Swain|first1=Stuart G.|title=Proof Without Words: Gabriel's Staircase|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=67|issue=3|year=2018|pages=209|issn=0025-570X|doi=10.1080/0025570X.1994.11996214}}</ref><ref name="Edgar2018">{{cite journal|last1=Edgar|first1=Tom|title=Staircase Series|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=91|issue=2|year=2018|pages=92–95|issn=0025-570X|doi=10.1080/0025570X.2017.1415584|s2cid=218542483 }}</ref> In general,

:<math>\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} {\color{blue} k} {\color{green} r^k} = \frac{r}{(1 - r)^2} \quad \text{for }-1<r<1.</math>


The label of arithmetico-geometric sequence may also be given to different objects combining characteristics of both arithmetic and geometric sequences. For instance, the [[:fr:Suite arithmético-géométrique|French notion of arithmetico-geometric sequence]] refers to sequences that satisfy [[Recurrence relation|recurrence relations]] of the form <math>u_{n+1}=r u_n+ d</math>, which combine the defining recurrence relations  <math>u_{n+1}=u_n+d</math> for arithmetic sequences and <math>u_{n+1}= r u_n</math> for geometric sequences. These sequences are therefore solutions to a special class of [[linear difference equation]]: inhomogeneous first order [[Linear recurrence with constant coefficients|linear recurrences with constant coefficients]].

==Elements==
The elements of an arithmetico-geometric sequence <math>(A_n G_n)_{n \geq 1}</math> are the products of the elements of an [[arithmetic progression]] <math>(A_n)_{n \geq 1}</math> (in blue) with initial value <math>a</math> and common difference <math>d</math>, <math>A_n = a + (n - 1)d,</math> with the corresponding elements of a [[geometric progression]] <math>(G_n)_{n \geq 1}</math> (in green) with initial value <math>b</math> and common ratio <math>r</math>, <math>G_n = b r^{n-1},</math> so that<ref name="RHB118">{{cite book |author1=K. F. Riley |author2=M. P. Hobson |author3=S. J. Bence |title= Mathematical methods for physics and engineering|url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalmeth00rile |url-access=registration |edition= 3rd|year= 2010|page=[https://archive.org/details/mathematicalmeth00rile/page/118 118]|publisher= Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-86153-3}}</ref>

: <math>
\begin{align}
A_1 G_1 & =\color{blue}a \color{green}b \\
A_2 G_2 & =\color{blue}(a+d) \color{green}br \\
A_3 G_3 & =\color{blue}(a+2d)\color{green} br^2 \\
& \ \,\vdots \\
A_n G_n & =\color{blue}\bigl(a+(n-1)d \bigr)\color{green} br^{n-1}\color{black}.
\end{align}
</math>
These four parameters are somewhat redundant and can be reduced to three: <math>ab, </math> <math>bd, </math> and <math>r. </math>

===Example===
The sequence

:<math>\frac{\color{blue}{0}}{\color{green}{1}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{1}}{\color{green}{2}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{2}}{\color{green}{4}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{green}{8}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{4}}{\color{green}{16}}, \ \frac{\color{blue}{5}}{\color{green}{32}}, \cdots </math>

is the arithmetico-geometric sequence with parameters <math>d=b=1</math>, <math>a=0</math>, and <math>r=\tfrac12</math>.

== Series ==

=== Partial sums ===
The sum of the first {{math|''n''}} terms of an arithmetico-geometric series has the form

: <math>
\begin{align}
S_n & = \sum_{k = 1}^n A_k G_k \\[5pt]
& = \sum_{k = 1}^n \bigl(a + (k - 1) d\bigr) br^{k - 1} \\[5pt]
& = b \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1} \left(a + k d\right) r^{k} \\[5pt]
& = ab + (a + d) br + (a + 2 d) br^2 + \cdots + \bigl(a + (n - 1) d\bigr) br^{n - 1}
\end{align}
</math>
where <math display="inline">A_i</math> and <math display="inline">G_i</math> are the {{mvar|i}}th elements of the arithmetic and the geometric sequence, respectively.

This partial sum has the [[closed-form expression]]
:<math>
\begin{align}
S_n & = \frac{ab - (a+nd)\,br^n}{1 - r}+\frac{dbr\,(1 - r^n)}{(1-r)^2}\\
    & = \frac{A_1G_1 - A_{n+1}G_{n+1}}{1 - r}+\frac{dr}{(1-r)^2}\,(G_1 - G_{n+1}).
\end{align}
</math>
son
==== Derivation ====
Multiplying<ref name="RHB118"/>
:<math>S_n = ab + (a + d) br + (a + 2 d) br^2 + \cdots + \bigl(a + (n - 1) d\bigr) br^{n - 1}</math>
by {{math|''r''}} gives
:<math>r S_n = a br + (a + d) br^2 + (a + 2 d) br^3 + \cdots + \bigl(a + (n - 1) d\bigr) br^n.</math>

Subtracting {{math|''rS<sub>n</sub>''}} from {{math|''S<sub>n</sub>''}}, dividing both sides by <math>b</math>, and using the technique of [[telescoping series]] (second equality) and the formula for the sum of a finite [[geometric series]] (fifth equality) gives
:<math>\begin{align} 
\frac{(1 - r) S_n}{b} &= \left(a + (a + d) r + (a + 2 d) r^2 + \cdots + \bigl(a + (n - 1) d\bigr) r^{n - 1}\right) - \Bigl(a r + (a + d) r^2 + (a + 2 d) r^3 + \cdots + \bigl(a + (n - 1) d\bigr) r^n\Bigr) \\[5pt]
&= a + d \left(r + r^2 + \cdots + r^{n-1}\right) - \bigl(a + (n - 1) d\bigr) r^n \\[5pt]
&= a + d \left(r + r^2 + \cdots + r^{n-1}+r^n\right) - \left(a + n d\right) r^n \\[5pt]
&= a + d r \left(1 + r + r^2 + \cdots + r^{n-1}\right) - \left(a + nd\right) r^n \\[5pt]
&= a + \frac{d r (1 - r^n)}{1 - r} - (a + nd) r^n, \\[8pt]
S_n &= \frac{b}{1-r} \left( a - (a + nd) r^n + \frac{d r (1 - r^n)}{1 - r} \right) \\[5pt]
&= \frac{ab - (a + nd) b r^n}{1-r} + \frac{d r (b - br^n)}{(1 - r)^2} \\[5pt]
&= \frac{A_1 G_1 - A_{n+1} G_{n+1}}{1-r} + \frac{d r (G_1 - G_{n+1})}{(1 - r)^2}
\end{align}</math>
as claimed.

=== Infinite series ===
If {{math|−1 < ''r'' < 1}}, then the sum {{math|''S''}} of the arithmetico-geometric [[Series (mathematics)|series]], that is to say, the [[Limit of a sequence|limit]] of the partial sums of the elements of the sequence, is given by<ref name="RHB118" />

:<math>
\begin{align}
S &= \sum_{k = 1}^\infty t_k = \lim_{n \to \infty}S_{n} \\[5pt]
  &= \frac{ab}{1-r}+\frac{dbr}{(1-r)^2}\\[5pt]
  &= \frac{A_1G_1}{1 - r}+\frac{d r G_1}{(1-r)^2}.
\end{align}
</math>

If {{math|''r''}} is outside of the above range, {{math|''b''}} is not zero, and {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''d''}} are not both zero, the limit does not exist and the series is [[Divergent series|divergent]].

===Example===
The sum

:<math>S=\frac{\color{blue}{0}}{\color{green}{1}}+\frac{\color{blue}{1}}{\color{green}{2}}+\frac{\color{blue}{2}}{\color{green}{4}}+\frac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{green}{8}}+\frac{\color{blue}{4}}{\color{green}{16}}+\frac{\color{blue}{5}}{\color{green}{32}}+\cdots </math>,

is the sum of an arithmetico-geometric series defined by <math>d=b=1</math>, <math>a=0</math>, and <math>r=\tfrac 12</math>, and it converges to <math>S=2</math>. This sequence corresponds to the expected number of [[Coin flipping|coin tosses]] required to obtain "tails". The probability <math>T_k</math> of obtaining tails for the first time at the ''k''th toss is as follows:

:<math>T_1=\frac 1{2}, \ T_2=\frac 1{4},\dots, T_k = \frac 1{2^k}</math>.

Therefore, the expected number of tosses to reach the first "tails" is given by

:<math>\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k T_k = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac {\color{blue}k}{\color{green}2^k} = 2.</math>
Similarly, the sum 

: <math>S=\frac{\color{blue}{0} \cdot \color{green}\frac16}{\color{green}\frac56}+\frac{\color{blue}{1} \cdot \color{green}\frac16}{\color{green}{1}}+\frac{\color{blue}{2} \cdot \color{green}\frac16}{\color{green}{\frac65}}+\frac{\color{blue}{3} \cdot \color{green}\frac16}{\color{green}{\left(\frac65\right)^2}}+\frac{\color{blue}{4} \cdot \color{green}\frac16}{\color{green}{\left(\frac65\right)^3}}+\frac{\color{blue}{5} \cdot \color{green}\frac16}{\color{green}{\left(\frac65\right)^4}}+\cdots</math>

is the sum of an arithmetico-geometric series defined by <math>d = 1 </math>, <math>a = 0 </math>, <math>b = \tfrac{1/6}{5/6} = \tfrac15 </math>, and <math>r = \tfrac56 </math>, and it converges to 6. This sequence corresponds to the expected number of [[six-sided dice]] rolls required to obtain a specific value on a die roll, for instance "5". In general, these series with <math>d = 1 </math>, <math>a = 0 </math>, <math>b = \tfrac{p}{1 - p} </math>, and <math>r = 1-p </math> give the expectations of "the number of trials until first success" in [[Bernoulli process|Bernoulli processes]] with "success probability" <math>p </math>. The probabilities of each outcome follow a [[geometric distribution]] and provide the geometric sequence factors in the terms of the series, while the number of trials per outcome provides the arithmetic sequence factors in the terms.
